clinicalPearls: Enteropathic arthritis is the inflammatory arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) and belongs to the seronegative spondyloarthritis family
It has two broad patterns, peripheral arthritis and axial (spinal and sacroiliac) disease, which may overlap in the same patient

Peripheral disease is subdivided into a type 1 pattern (pauciarticular, large-joint, asymmetrical, often flaring with bowel activity and self-limiting) and a type 2 pattern (polyarticular, small-joint, more persistent, and largely independent of bowel activity)
Axial involvement (sacroiliitis and spondylitis) resembles ankylosing spondylitis, may be asymptomatic or cause inflammatory back pain, and runs a course independent of the gut inflammation
Extra-articular spondyloarthritis features may occur, including enthesitis, dactylitis, anterior uveitis, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum
The condition is seronegative (rheumatoid factor negative), and HLA-B27 is associated particularly with the axial disease

Management coordinates treatment of the bowel and joint disease: controlling gut inflammation helps type 1 peripheral disease, physiotherapy and appropriate therapy address axial disease, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are used cautiously as they may aggravate colitis, and certain biologic agents such as anti-tumour necrosis factor drugs treat both gut and joints
reference.pathophysiology: In genetically predisposed individuals, including carriers of HLA-B27 for the axial phenotype, inflammation of the gut mucosa in inflammatory bowel disease is thought to allow translocation of luminal antigens and trafficking of activated immune cells that promote inflammation at the joints, entheses, and axial skeleton. This shared gut-joint immune axis links intestinal and musculoskeletal inflammation and places the disorder within the spondyloarthritis spectrum, helping explain why type 1 peripheral disease often parallels bowel activity while axial disease pursues an independent course.
additionalDifferentials: Gout or CPP crystal arthritis in acute peripheral joint presentations
Arthralgia related to inflammatory bowel disease therapy
additionalInvestigations: Inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein and ESR) and faecal calprotectin to gauge bowel activity
HLA-B27 testing, especially where there are axial features
Radiographs and MRI of the sacroiliac joints and spine for sacroiliitis and spondylitis
Radiographs or ultrasound of affected peripheral joints and entheses
Joint aspiration with microscopy and culture to exclude crystal or septic arthritis
Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies to help exclude rheumatoid arthritis
Colonoscopy and gastroenterology assessment to confirm and monitor the inflammatory bowel disease
redFlags: A hot swollen joint that could represent septic arthritis rather than a flare
New or worsening axial symptoms with neurological features
Acute anterior uveitis (a painful red eye) requiring urgent ophthalmology review
Severe bowel disease activity or complications needing gastroenterology input
reference.prognosis: Type 1 peripheral arthritis is usually self-limiting and improves as the bowel disease is controlled, whereas type 2 peripheral and axial disease tend to be more persistent and can, like ankylosing spondylitis, lead to structural spinal damage if untreated; the overall outlook is improved by coordinated control of both gut and joint inflammation.
pitfalls: Using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs freely for the arthritis without recognising they can worsen colitis
Treating the joints in isolation and neglecting the underlying bowel disease, or vice versa
Missing axial disease because it runs independently of gut symptoms
Overlooking coexisting septic or crystal arthritis in an acutely inflamed joint
Attributing all joint symptoms to the bowel disease without excluding other spondyloarthropathies
management: Treat the underlying inflammatory bowel disease, since controlling gut inflammation often settles type 1 peripheral arthritis, using aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, thiopurines and biologics chosen jointly with gastroenterology
Physiotherapy and a regular exercise programme to preserve spinal mobility and function, particularly in axial disease
Intra-articular corticosteroid injections for isolated active peripheral joints, using systemic NSAIDs cautiously as they may provoke bowel flares

Escalate persistent peripheral or axial disease to anti-TNF monoclonal antibodies such as infliximab or adalimumab that treat both joints and gut, avoiding etanercept which does not control the bowel disease
Prompt ophthalmology referral and topical corticosteroids for acute anterior uveitis
Monitor disease activity with C-reactive protein and faecal calprotectin and screen for structural sacroiliac and spinal damage on imaging
Coordinated rheumatology and gastroenterology multidisciplinary follow-up
